01

What this thing is

A staffing agency's revenue engine

It watches the job market for signs a company is quietly struggling to hire, ranks those companies by how likely the demand is, matches your candidates against the roles, drafts the proposal, and tracks the deal through to placement. A manager dashboard sits on top with the three numbers the business runs on.

The line it deliberately does not cross: the AI drafts, a human sends. There is no outbound path in the code at all, and Megan proved that by disabling every possible one and showing nothing fires.

Where it stands

17 of 20 stories are built. Releases R0 through R3 are complete: the foundation, the demand board, the sales pipeline with the human release gate, and the analytics and compliance layer. What is left is R4, launch readiness: load testing, end-to-end tests, and what was going to be a public demo.

Your three approval gates cover work that is already finished. The oldest has been open 22 days.

Read the pictures with this in mind

Only 3 of the 32 screenshots below show the actual interface. The other 29 are terminal output: test suites passing, migrations running, code under review. Each one is labelled so you can tell them apart at a glance.

That is not padding on her part, it is what she was asked for. Every story required proof that the acceptance criteria passed, and she supplied it thoroughly. But it does mean there is very little visual record of the product itself, which is worth knowing before you approve it, and is exactly what the recorded walkthrough now on her plate will fix.

02

Where this project came from

Worth reading first if you do not remember commissioning it.

Created
2026-07-21 at 15:06, under Ali's Basecamp identity.
Generated from
A 160 KB document, TalentSignal Revenue Engine - Build Guide v1, dated the same day and still attached in the project's Docs & Files folder.
How that document was made
It reads as machine output, not something written by hand. Its opening profile is a set of slugs: Problem: hidden_demand, Target User: staffing_agencies, Value Proposition: proactive_sales, Monetization: subscription_fee. That is the shape the AI Project Architect produces when it expands a short idea into a full build guide.
How it became a Basecamp plan
The story-build pipeline turned the guide into 20 requirements, 20 stories across 5 releases, and the to-do list Megan has been working from. That pipeline runs identity-guarded as Ali, which is why every document and the list itself show him as the author.
So the chain was: a short idea, expanded by one tool into a build guide, expanded by a second tool into a work plan, published under Ali's name. It is entirely possible for this project to exist, and to be well specified, without Ali having consciously specified it. That is worth knowing before judging the work inside it.

Three features in the source guide never became requirements

The Build Guide lists Automated Email Follow-ups, Client Engagement Tools and Real-time Analytics among its selected features. None of them appear in the 20 requirements.

Dropping the email follow-ups was the right call and probably deliberate: automatic outbound email would directly contradict REQ-020, the rule that nothing leaves the platform without a human releasing it. The other two simply fell away between the two documents.

The short version

17 of 20 requirements are met outright. Every single "must" is met except two, and both gaps are in the same place: launch readiness, which she has not started.

REQ-017 (performance) is not built, and has also been amended: authentication is now scoped out of the 200ms budget, because bcrypt exceeds it by design and weakening it would trade real security for a metric.

REQ-018 (deployment) is partial and can no longer be met as written: Docker is done, CI and end-to-end tests are not started, and the public demo URL was cancelled on 2026-08-12. It needs rewording to a recorded local walkthrough.

The mocked-data question, answered precisely

The demand board ranks companies on invented signals. That is real, and it is why the demo is hard to follow: there is no provenance to show behind any row.

But it is not a gap someone forgot. REQ-019 says, in the requirements document itself, "pull job-board and market signals through provider adapters (mocked for the demo)". Megan built exactly what she was asked for, and built the adapter seam a real source would plug into. The decision to run on mocked data was made in the requirements on day one, not by her.

It remains the single biggest thing standing between this and something real, and no story in the plan changes it.

Two stories shipped with no evidence at all

S-13 (predictive analysis) and S-15 (data privacy and audit trail) are both marked complete with no write-up comment and no screenshots, unlike the other fifteen. S-15 is the GDPR and CCPA requirement, so that is the one place the missing evidence actually matters. Worth asking her for the verification on that one specifically before approving Phase 2.

S-02

People can register and log in securely.

S-02 - Secure authentication (register / login, JWT)
Built

Why it matters. Without accounts there are no roles, and without roles nothing else can be restricted.

Worth knowing. She closed two attacks that were not in the spec: one that let you discover which email addresses exist, and a timing trick that leaks the same thing. She proved passwords never reach the logs by scanning all output for the raw text.

Megan's own write-up and verification
S-02 complete

Register and login use a users table. The login returns a signed JWT that carries the user ID and role. Both acceptance scenarios pass. The trust scenario is verified by a test that registers with a unique password and checks that the raw string does not appear anywhere in the captured stdout. This includes a full-text scan, so it also catches leaks in error messages and stack traces.

Two attacks were closed that weren't included in the spec: user enumeration, where a wrong password and unknown email return byte-identical 401s with the same body, Content-Length, and ETag, and the timing side-channel related to this. Both paths run a bcrypt compare, using a dummy hash when the email isn't found. This means that an unknown email does not return faster.

Email uniqueness is enforced by a database constraint and not by a check-then-insert method. This was verified against the live container by firing two simultaneous registrations, which returned exactly [201, 409] and one row.

Registration hardcodes the role of sales. An admin is set up from environment variables. If the registration accepted a role from the body, anyone could make themselves an admin, and S-14's RBAC would be useless.

Thirty tests pass and three skip by design. The TypeScript compiler has no errors. Decisions 002–006 are logged.

Two things were noted:

There is a requirements conflict. REQ-017 sets the 95th percentile under 200ms, but bcrypt at cost 12 exceeds that on its own. The slowness is part of the security mechanism. I don’t think authentication should be weakened to meet a general performance target. I propose we limit REQ-017 to data endpoints and exempt authentication explicitly. This needs your written decision.
No recruiter account can exist until S-14. Registration is sales-only, and the bootstrap creates one admin. Therefore, there isn't a recruiter to demonstrate with. I'm flagging this before it surprises us at a gate.

R1 - Core intelligence surfaces

4 / 4 built

The actual product appears. Companies ranked by hidden hiring demand, real client and candidate records behind it, and candidates ranked against a job.

S-04

The demand board: companies ranked by how likely they are to be hiring.

S-04 - Hidden Demand Analysis service
Built

Why it matters. This is the product. Everything before it was foundation; this is the screen a salesperson opens in the morning.

Worth knowing. She found the first version wrote to the database once per record in a loop, which would never survive real volume, and replaced it with a single bulk write. 10,000 records in about 0.7 seconds against a 5 second target.

Megan's own write-up and verification
S-04 complete

The platform now ranks companies based on likely hidden staffing demand. A set of signals is scored, ranked by highest confidence first, and displayed on the demand board. Each opportunity includes its confidence, reasons, and source. It reuses S-03's scorer unchanged; there is no second scoring engine.

Both acceptance scenarios pass. Ranked, explainable opportunities are ordered by bounded confidence with contributing factors, using a stable unique ID to break ties. Latency was measured at about 700ms for 10,000 seed records, which is around seven times faster than the five-second target.

The change that allowed for 10,000 records: S-03 wrote each opportunity in its own database call inside a loop, which was not feasible at scale. S-04 replaces this with a single batched unnest upsert. This uses one array per column, zipped into rows inside Postgres in one atomic statement. It also avoids Postgres's 65,535-parameter limit that a naive multi-row VALUES statement would hit at this scale.

For the trust scenario — "the platform never contacts a client on its own" — a test monitors every outbound path and confirms that none are triggered during analysis. It will correctly start to fail when S-09 adds the real release gate, requiring a conscious decision then.

Two honest notes: the confidence weights are still my proposal awaiting review (decision 007) and have become crucial since the entire board ranks by them. Latency is measured server-side, not by wall clock. Local timing was unreliable under memory pressure, so final sign-off should occur in CI and officially in S-18.

There are 48 backend tests, 12 frontend tests, and tsc clean. Starting S-05.

S-05

Clients, candidates and job openings can be managed.

S-05 - Clients and candidates: data model and management
Built

Why it matters. The real records the rest of the system reasons about.

Worth knowing. Personal data is tagged at the database level, and a salesperson simply does not receive candidate contact details in the response. She separated "this is personal data" from "hide this", so a candidate name stays visible for matching while still being erasable later.

Megan's own write-up and verification
S-05 complete.

Three main entities are modeled: clients, candidates, and job openings. We have typed Express CRUD and React management screens, and records include created and updated timestamps.

In the trust scenario, personally identifiable information (PII) is flagged at the schema level and restricted by access roles. A pii_fields registry table indicates which columns contain personal data. This table is seeded in the same migration that creates the columns, following TBI rule 7. For field-level redaction, a sales user receives a candidate record with contact_info removed, while a recruiter or admin can see it. This is confirmed by automated tests: pii.redaction.test.ts and pii.contactInfoLogSafety.test.ts both pass.

Two design decisions are worth noting, both recorded and added to my list for your return:

Marking and hiding are different actions. The registry records what is considered PII (allowing S-15 to handle erasure requests) separately from what to hide from view. A candidate's name is marked as PII (erasable) but remains visible to enable matchmaking. A client's name is a company name, which is not personal data, so it is excluded. (decision 009)
Recruiter accounts. There was no option to create a recruiter since registration hardcodes to sales, and bootstrap creates one admin. I added an admin-only create-user route instead of reopening self-registration to allow role input. (decision 010)

Eighty-three backend tests pass, twelve frontend tests pass, and tsc shows no errors. Log safety has been extended, so contact information does not appear in the logs, similar to passwords.

One item has been deferred: the registry-coverage test and a manual sales versus recruiter walkthrough are database-gated and require a running Postgres session. The automated redaction and log safety tests already demonstrate control. Starting S-06.

S-06

Given a job, the system ranks the candidates who fit it.

S-06 - Client Matchmaking (ranked candidates for a job)
Built

Why it matters. The matchmaking core. It is what a recruiter would otherwise do by memory.

Worth knowing. Every ranking comes with the reasons behind it, not just a number.

Megan's own write-up and verification
S-06 is complete.

When there is a job opening, the platform ranks candidates based on their fit and explains the reasoning. Fit uses a skills-overlap method called the Ochiai coefficient, which is calculated as |matching skills| / √(|candidate skills| × |job requirements|). Experience is combined in a way that increases the score based on skill relevance. However, it never acts as an independent factor; a candidate with no matching skills will receive a score of 0 and cannot rank higher than someone with relevant skills.

In the trust scenario, a human makes the final decision while the platform offers suggestions. Each result is marked as a suggestion, which is enforced in the system rather than just in the user interface. Each fit score displays which skills matched, and there is a test that ensures no candidate is automatically submitted anywhere. This test will begin to fail once S-09 adds the human-release gate, serving as an intentional tripwire.

Two judgment calls are logged for your review (decision 011): the proposed skills/experience weight split is 0.7/0.3, and the saturation cap is established. Currently, availability is for display only since it is freeform text without a defined vocabulary; I did not want to create filter rules for undefined values.

Additionally, the match endpoint never returns contact information for any role. This is intentionally stricter than the candidates screen, as this endpoint focuses on ranking rather than retrieving contacts. This is secured by a dedicated test.

The results show that 105 backend tests have passed, 15 frontend tests have also passed, and the TypeScript code is clean.

S-07

Opportunities get a score so the best ones surface first.

S-07 - Opportunity Scoring System
Built

Why it matters. Turns a long list into a prioritised queue.

Worth knowing. Reuses the same scorer as the earlier stories rather than introducing a second one, so the numbers cannot drift apart.

Megan's own write-up and verification
S-07 complete
Each opportunity is now assigned a consistent and auditable score. Most important, S-07 includes no new scoring formula since scoreSignal() remains the only place where a score is ever calculated. The innovation lies in making the score inspectable—this involves a structured breakdown that shows the weight, value, and contribution of each factor (not just the reason strings) and is accompanied by a weight version so that the score can remain traceable when the weights are finally approved or modified.
In the trust scenario the process is auditable rather than a black box since each score response includes its factors and the version of the weight; the board provides a detailed breakdown for each row which a manager can expand. Moreover, the process is deterministic because a test confirms that the factor contributions add up exactly to the score, so the breakdown and the score can never differ.
Idempotent: when the same input is provided, the result and the breakdown are identical, having been verified. (In the idempotency test, the scoring fields are compared, not the row timestamps, since the updated_at field is legitimately altered during a re-analysis.)
In decision 012 there is one honest limitation: opportunities which were scored before S-07 have no stored breakdown and therefore cannot be reconstructed (the original signal was never saved), so they are regarded as non-auditable rather than being given a fake breakdown. Since the demo uses a clean database all the opportunities that are visible have a real breakdown.
The weight versioning is recorded as decision 012; the weights remain as in decision 007 and are still awaiting your review. 132 tests pass and the TSC is clean. We are now proceeding with R2.

R2 - Pipeline and human-in-the-loop

4 / 4 built

Where it becomes a working sales tool, and where the trust line gets drawn: the AI drafts, a human releases. Nothing leaves the platform on its own.

S-08

A sales pipeline: opportunities move through stages.

S-08 - Sales Pipeline Management
Built

Why it matters. The day-to-day workflow a sales manager lives in.

Worth knowing. Every stage change is written to a log the database itself prevents anyone from editing afterwards. That append-only guarantee is enforced below the application, so a bug in the app cannot rewrite history.

Megan's own write-up and verification
The S-08 has been completed—this action opens R2 and provides the audit-trail basis for the compliance work carried out in R3.

A sales representative moves a client from one stage to another on a kanban board, recording with each transition an audit entry that shows who made the move and when it was made together with the stage it was moved from and to.

In the case of trust, the audit log is append-only and this is enforced by the database, not by convention. A trigger prevents any UPDATE or DELETE operations from being carried out on the audit rows. I checked this using a real instance of Postgres: the integration test attempts a direct UPDATE and DELETE on the audit table and finds that the database rejects both of them. (I also made sure that a simple REVOKE wouldn't work in this situation—our single Postgres role is a superuser and also the owner of the table, so it would circumvent the privilege checks; meanwhile, the trigger operates outside of that mechanism and is able to stop even a superuser.)

Other cases included a concurrency race in which when two representatives were enrolling the same new client at the same time an inaccurate audit row could be written – this was resolved by using a transaction-scoped advisory lock and has been verified by a real test involving two connections. The notification hook triggers internally but sends no messages externally (this is controlled by S-09's human-release gate), having been confirmed by a test with no outbound messages.

The following two judgments apply to you: since real deals can be reversed, stage transitions are freeform (that is, it is possible to move from any stage to any other stage) rather than following a strict sequence (as specified in decision 014); and although changed_by is classified as PII it is marked as exempt from erasure regarding retention, because deleting an audit trail would undermine its purpose – this constitutes a standard privacy exemption (decision 013).

131 tests pass, this figure including those of the database-backed integration tests and the tsc clean.

S-09

The AI drafts a proposal. A human sends it. Never the machine.

S-09 - AI-drafted opportunity packages under human release
Built

Why it matters. She calls this the keystone, and she is right: it is the line between a useful assistant and something that emails your clients on its own.

Worth knowing. She proved it by disabling every outbound path and showing nothing fires, during drafting and during release. Releasing requires a deliberate human action, and who released it and when is recorded permanently.

Megan's own write-up and verification
S-09 is complete—it's the keystone. By code designation this is REQ-020: the AI prepares the draft but a human carries out the sending.

The sales representative selects an opportunity and a job opening; the PackageAgent then prepares a proposal by using the S-06 matchmaking logic to include the top three candidates along with the reasons for their suitability and saves it as a draft marked AI-generated. The proposal is not sent anywhere since there is no email sent, no entry made in the CRM, and no outbound process present in the code.

The two aspects of the trust scenario have been verified: (a) a drafted package is stored, marked as AI-generated, and then delivered to no one—this test shuts down all outbound mechanisms and shows that no calls are made either when the draft is being processed or when it is released; (b) in order to release something an explicit human POST is required, this POST records both who carried out the release and when it took place, with the information being written to an append-only audit table that is protected by the database against tampering (this is the same trigger pattern as in S-08). This has been checked using real Postgres.

The term "released" always means "a human has authorized it to leave" — no action is taken as a result of that authorization. According to your build note, the release flag serves as the boundary; a subsequent sender will check it before sending. The action of re-releasing is rejected and the original actor and timestamp are never overwritten.

Two judgment calls have been recorded (decision numbers 015 and 016): the draft specifies that both opportunityId and jobOpeningId are required since there is currently no foreign key link between opportunities and job openings, and the top-candidate-count is 3, which is proposed for your approval.

We also identified and resolved a previous bug that was causing the demo to break: the auth rate limiter had been set to apply to all routes under /api rather than just those for login and register, which meant that a few page reloads would result in the entire app being returned a 429 response. The limiter has now been properly scoped, together with a regression test.

148 tests pass and tsc is clean. We'll start S-10.

S-10

Finds warm introductions: who already knows someone at the target company.

S-10 - Warm Relationship Identification
Built

Why it matters. A warm path is worth more than any amount of cold outreach.

Worth knowing. Deliberately simple, no graph database, because you asked for lightweight. Confidence multiplies along the chain, so one weak link drags the whole path down and a direct relationship always beats a two-hop guess.

Megan's own write-up and verification
S-10 complete.

To provide an opportunity, the platform displays warm introduction paths through the relationship graph, each path being ranked and including a confidence level together with the people who connect them. Since you mentioned keeping it lightweight, it uses a simple edges table, computes the 1–2 hop paths directly in memory, and does not make use of a graph database.

In the trust scenario a human has to approve it before it is taken into account: each path is marked as an advisory guess together with its level of confidence, and the recruiter either confirms or rejects it. There is a real recorded difference between confirmation and no confirmation (nothing currently acts on it, just as with the release flag). Unlike in the case of release, confirmation or rejection is reversible since it controls an internal signal rather than something that leaves the platform.

Confidence is a transparent multiplicative score (since a weak link causes the entire path's score to drop and a direct strong relationship always takes precedence over a two-hop guess), together with a breakdown of the factors — it is never just a single number.

It is worth mentioning one point regarding correctness: since a path's identity is defined as a canonical (sorted) set of edge ids, the path remains confirmed even when the page is reloaded, no matter what the order of traversal is—this has been verified by a regression test that intentionally returns the edges in a different order.

The honest limitation has been recorded (decision 017): a client is matched to an opportunity based on company name, which is why a name mismatch results in zero paths being found—fuzzy matching has not yet been implemented. The weights suggested are waiting for your approval (decision 018).

162 tests pass and tsc is clean; starting with S-11, which is the last one in R2.

S-11

Recruiters rate recommendations good or bad, and it is remembered.

S-11 - Recommendation Engine with feedback loop
Built

Why it matters. The beginning of the system learning from the people using it.

The candidate recommendations include a rationale written in plain English as well as a thumbs feedback control; the ranking makes use of S-06's matchmaking exactly—the scoreCandidate is imported without any changes, with no new scoring logic being introduced; the recommend test reuses the ranking assertions that were provided by S-06 in order to show that nothing about the scoring has drifted.

The process is reversible (good and bad can be upsized in either direction) and the entire thing is verified end-to-end within the browser. As you've described it, the signal is stored but no retraining takes place at this stage — we store it now and will tune it later.

The latency was 82ms when processing 5,000 candidates, which is well below the 2-second target (AC-4-9).

There is one question that I have for you (decision 019): the feedback table retains only the most recent rating for each recruiter, not a full history. While this does mean that the feedback is stored, your TBI note states that feedback is captured "in order to correct bias over time" – a requirement which in the future might demand the full history. S-12 - Reporting and Analytics dashboard
Built

Why it matters. The three numbers an agency manager actually runs the business on.

Megan's own write-up and verification
The S-12 is complete, marking the first R3 story and also my first dashboard.

For an agency manager there are three key performance indicators: the number of placements each month (as recorded), time-to-hire, and demand score—all of which are calculated in real time from actual data and not from made-up figures. The figures for placements and time-to-hire are taken from the S-08 append-only audit trail (the timestamps in it are the genuine record of when events took place); the demand score is the average opportunity confidence.

In the trust scenario—where aggregates never leak personally identifiable information—the dashboard displays only counts, averages, and rates, without showing the name or contact details of any individual candidate. This has been proven by a test that reads the pii_fields registry and confirms that no registered column containing PII appears anywhere in the analytics response, so the statement remains correct automatically as new stories in the future register additional PII. The scenario has been verified using real Postgres.

Since I am the human who owns this case (you've marked it as such 🧑), I have made two decisions, both of which are currently listed as pending your approval (decision 020): counting placements as closing events each month (in this case, each reopen and reclose counts as two — this is an accurate reflection of the actual activity), and setting the time-to-hire as the period from a client's first entry into the pipeline to each close.

Regarding your call, there is one intentional exception: although your build note states "Model an Analytics table", I have instead calculated the KPIs on the fly — this is because the queries involved are simple and inexpensive, and setting up a stored snapshot table would only introduce staleness without any users needing it, as there's no current requirement for KPI history over time. The change is completely reversible if you'd rather have the table, and it's highlighted at the top of my open-questions list so that it can be seen rather than being hidden.

S-14

Roles decide what each person can see and do.

S-14 - Role-Based Access Control
Built

Why it matters. A recruiter, a salesperson and an admin should not see the same system.

Worth knowing. Enforced on the server, not just hidden in the interface, which is the difference between real access control and a cosmetic one.

Megan's own write-up and verification
S-14 complete.

The roles (admin, sales, recruiter) are now enforced on all routes through the use of an explicit permission matrix — in this way 'any role' has become a deliberate and documented choice rather than an unintended situation caused by nobody setting up a gate. The existing requireRole middleware is being reused again, with no new authentication mechanism being introduced. The matrix is being logged as decision 022 and is currently under proposal for your review, with the entries having lower confidence being flagged so that you can go directly to them.

Trust scenario — ownership, not just role: this has been handled honestly. I have gone through each migration and found that only one table (the recommendation feedback table) has schema-backed per-user ownership; the other actor columns are accountability fields relating to shared resources, and therefore it would be wrong to gate access to them since the workflow does not support such a restriction — deliberately excluded and recorded. In order to make the ownership scenario real and testable, I included one small route (GET /recommendation-engine/feedback) such that when a non-admin user requests another recruiter's data they receive a 403 response — this new user interface element is clearly indicated in decision 022 as having been added for that purpose, not as a hidden addition.

When refusals occur, a 403 error message is returned and the event is recorded together with the user's name, their role, and the route involved. React screens are also restricted according to role (for example, a recruiter never sees the sales pipeline board) — but the actual security boundary is provided by the backend matrix; the user interface merely offers convenience.

In response to your note — "test the unauthorized path, not just the happy one" — all newly gated routes include a test in which a wrong role results in a 403 response, together with a test on ownership denial and another one verifying that a denial is logged.

The verification exercise using the actual database shows that 213 tests pass, there are zero failures, and the DB-gated integration tests (those involving append-only operations, concurrency, and PII) still pass when the new role enforcement is applied — which is exactly the aim of the story. tsc clean.

S-16

Stops the CRM filling with duplicates, and lets a bad write be undone.

S-16 - CRM Pollution Prevention
Built

Why it matters. Data quality is what makes every number above trustworthy.

Worth knowing. This is where she found the contradiction nobody asked her to look for: a rollback could restore data somebody had legally erased. She refused to exempt the snapshots and raised it rather than picking the convenient answer.

Megan's own write-up and verification
S-16 — CRM Pollution Prevention — done ✅

The CRM's write operations are now idempotent and reversible. Each write includes an idempotency key; if the same key is used again, the stored result is returned without having to reapply it (thus eliminating duplicates), a feature that has been verified at the database level. A faulty write can be rolled back to the exact previous known-good state, and a rollback can be performed only once. Both each write and each rollback are recorded in an append-only audit table (the same insert-only trigger as in S-08/S-15).

Verification identified and resolved an actual bug: when an unknown client id was given, it was returning a 500 rather than a 404 since the foreign key check had been carried out before my existence check; this is now handled by returning a 404, just like the rest of the API.

The full suite consisted of 232 tests that passed and 0 that failed, with all four new tests being run against a real Postgres (the tests were run twice, rollback-trust and append-only modes were used, and concurrent deduping was enabled). There were no regressions.

At the next gate you will be asked to consider the following question: the rollback maintains a before-and-after snapshot of the client record, which contains contact details. This raises a conflict with the right under S-15 to have your data erased—if a person erases their data, should the rollback then be able to restore it? I did not indicate that these snapshots should be exempt (because that would allow a rollback to undo a legal erasure). I have recorded this as an open policy issue in decision 024, with my position being that 'erasure should win'—this is the counterpart to the still-open question in decision 015.

S-17 - Revenue anomaly detection and client segmentation
Built

Why it matters. Tells the manager where the money is behaving oddly.

Worth knowing. Closes out the analytics and trust release.

Megan's own write-up and verification
S-17 — Revenue anomaly detection + client segmentation — done ✅ (last R3 story)

There is one endpoint that includes two features. When a revenue figure moves outside its normal range, an anomaly detector triggers an alert and at the same time indicates what 'normal' was so that the alert can be understood. A human operator can either confirm or suppress each alert; if the alert is suppressed, the range is widened by a fixed, logged amount (with a cap applied in one direction) so that false alarms gradually disappear — this is a transparent rule, not a black box. Client segmentation involves grouping clients according to their hiring volume, with the result being shown to a human but never leading to any automated actions.

You need to raise this point: the schema doesn't have a revenue or money column anywhere. Instead of making up figures in dollars, I have used 'placements per month' as a named stand-in for revenue (the figure series that we already forecast in S-13) and have indicated this in decision 025. If genuine revenue is to be tracked, then that would require a new field and a judgment about what a deal is worth—something which is outside the scope of this story, but which is up to you to decide.

Suite 230 ran and produced zero failures, with the type checking passing. Three tests involving the database (including the suppress-and-learn trust scenario) have been written and are waiting for a Docker run on my machine.

What to do with this

The three gates are the easy part

Phases 1 and 2 cover R0 through R3, which are built and evidenced above. Phase 3 covers R4, which has not started, so that one is genuinely premature and can wait.

One story just changed under her

S-20 was "deploy to a public demo URL", and there will now be no hosted demo. That story needs rewriting to a recorded local walkthrough before she reaches R4, or she will start work against criteria that no longer hold.

What her open decisions are actually asking

Decision 019 (S-11): the feedback table keeps only the latest rating per recruiter, not the full history. She flagged that the stated intent, correcting bias over time, might eventually need the history, and asked rather than assuming.

That pattern is the thing worth noticing across this whole build. Three separate times she hit a point where the convenient answer was available and the honest one cost her time, and she took the honest one each time: refusing to weaken password security to hit a latency target, refusing to invent scoring weights when you went quiet, and refusing to let a rollback restore data someone had legally erased.
